# Final Touches — Murim Login

## Goal

Prepare one mastered chapter for readers. This pass adds footnotes, repairs formatting, and fixes duplicate or missing sentences. It is not a fluency rewrite.

Keep the mastered prose. Change a sentence only to attach a footnote, repair System / thought / speech / chat formatting, restore a source sentence the English dropped, or remove an English sentence the Korean does not support.

## Duplicates and omissions

Compare the English with the Korean source.

- Restore source facts, events, dialogue, and sentences the English dropped, in the same place in the scene.
- Remove English sentences that have no support in the Korean.
- Keep a bold label that names a quoted document, manual, warning, or sign, such as `> **Warning**`. Keep it when this chapter recalls or reprints a notice that was labeled earlier, even if the Korean reprint shows only the body.
- Keep repetition the Korean itself repeats: comedy, panic, emphasis, echoed dialogue, and short beats such as `……`.
- Do not treat a short refrain or a deliberate echo as a duplicate.

## Footnotes

Use Markdown footnotes (`[^1]`, `[^2]`, …). Number them in order of first appearance, starting at 1 for this chapter. Put every definition in one block at the end of the file.

Within this chapter, write one definition for a term, unit, amount, or reference. Every later occurrence of that same thing reuses the same marker. `goshiwon` five times is one note, and so is `hyung`. A different amount or a different term gets its own note. Another chapter may carry its own note for the same term.

Write notes in factual English. No spoilers and no jokes added by the note. Romanize words. A note may include the original character when it is explaining that character. Keep Hangul jamo already used as chat reactions, such as ㅋㅋ and ㄷㄷ.

Add a note only when an English reader would otherwise miss the meaning or the conversion. Skip it when the sentence already says what the reference means. A translated proverb whose warning is plain, a joke the next line completes, a place name used as a place, and a fictional law the dialogue already describes do not get notes.

Skip a conversion footnote when the prose already states both metric and imperial for that quantity.

### Won

Footnote Korean won, including round figures and vague amounts (“hundreds of millions of won”), when the prose does not already give the conversion. Use only the project rates in the packet. Show dollars, then euros, as approximate figures. Round large amounts to about two significant figures and say “about.” For a vague amount, give the approximate range those words cover. One note per distinct amount; reuse it for every later mention of that same amount.

Do not convert traditional money (nyang, taels, cash) or Chinese yuan with the won rate. Explain those with a cultural or historical note only when the English does not already carry the meaning.

### Units

Footnote a Korean or Chinese traditional unit, or a metric quantity, once in the chapter, with both metric and imperial, using this table:

| Unit | Use | Metric | Imperial |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pyeong (평) | area | 3.31 m² | 35.6 ft² |
| geun (근) | Korean weight | 600 g | 1.32 lb |
| ja / cheok (자) | length | 30.3 cm | 11.9 in |
| chi (치) | length | 3.03 cm | 1.19 in |
| don (돈) | weight | 3.75 g | 0.132 oz |
| gwan (관) | weight | 3.75 kg | 8.27 lb |
| ri (리), Korea | distance | 393 m | 0.244 mi |
| li (里), China | distance | 500 m | 0.311 mi |
| jin (斤), modern Chinese | weight | 500 g | 1.10 lb |
| liang (两), modern Chinese | weight | 50 g | 1.76 oz |

Choose Korean ri or Chinese li from the setting. Say which one the note uses.

Also footnote metric quantities already in the English (kilometers, meters, centimeters, kilograms, grams, liters, square meters, degrees Celsius) with the imperial equivalent. Use unit words or abbreviations (`ft`, `in`, `mi`, `lb`, `oz`, `gal`). Do not use `"` or `'` as unit marks.

### Cultural references

Footnote a Korean, Chinese, or other Asian word, custom, institution, food, joke, or allusion when the English does not already carry it: `goshiwon`, `hyung`, `doenjang`, `jeonse`. Explain it in one or two sentences. One note per term in the chapter, reused by every later occurrence.

Leave it unnoted when the English is already clear. Do not explain a proverb the translation has already stated, a pun the scene completes, or ordinary vocabulary.

Do not footnote standing series vocabulary. Never add a note whose job is to define any of these, including ordinary variants and compounds:

- Murim
- qi, including demonic qi, innate qi, and qi deviation
- dantian, including the Upper, Middle, and Lower Dantian
- internal energy
- mana

A note about something else may mention these words. Do not attach a marker to them.

## Formatting

Enforce these four patterns. Repair System, speech, thought, and chat formatting when it drifts. Leave every other blockquote heading as it stands.

- **System.** Each real game System panel is one Markdown blockquote headed exactly `> **System**`. Keep the panel’s lines inside that blockquote. Start a new panel only when prose intervenes. Do not wrap System text in square brackets or label a manual, sign, or ordinary quotation as System. A manual or remembered notice keeps its own label, such as `> **Warning**` or `> **Product User Manual**`. That label is not a System panel, and it is not drift.
- **Speech.** Spoken dialogue uses curly double quotes (`“` `”`). Not straight quotes, not italics.
- **Thoughts.** Direct thoughts are italics with no quotation marks.
- **Chat and comments.** Public comment threads and private chat logs shown as threads are one blockquote. Each message line begins with `└`, as in `> └ **Name:** message`. Keep a thread title that is not itself a message, such as `> **Peace Guild**`, on its own line above the messages. Do not add a `**Chat**` heading. A status line that is only a name or level, such as `> **Lv. 22 Hyuk Mujin**`, is not a chat message. Leave that line unchanged, including the bold. Ordinary spoken dialogue stays in curly quotes.
- **Headings.** The only Markdown heading is `# Chapter N`. Do not add `##` or `###`. A diary title or similar label stays a bold line, `**Training Day 1**`, even when the mastered copy used a smaller heading.

Leave narration as narration. Scene breaks stay `* * *`, with the same count as the source.

## Output contract

Return only the complete English Markdown chapter. The first nonblank line must be `# Chapter N`. No status line and no model preamble. Do not add Hangul syllables. Chat jamo and a character cited in a note may stay.

## Project conversion rates

These rates are binding. Do not look up or substitute a market rate.

- 1 US dollar = 1400 Korean won
- 1 euro = 1550 Korean won

Convert every won amount with these rates. In each footnote, give dollars first and euros second.

```text
＃178화



“객잔이 낡았군. 비가 새.”

나는 애꿎은 천장만 바라봤다.

“여기가 좀 낡긴 했죠.”

물론 비는 내리지 않았고 먹빛 하늘은 잠잠했다.

낡은 건 객잔이 아니라 적천강의 마음이다. 오래전의 아픈 추억을 떠올리니 그의 눈에서 비가 샌 것이다.

‘피도 눈물도 없는 노인네인 줄 알았는데.’

화왕 적천강.

저 괴팍한 성격의 초절정 고수에게 이런 과거가 있을 줄은 몰랐다. 그저 미친놈이라고 생각했던 조필에 대해서도 평가를 수정해야 했다.

‘상상 이상으로 미친놈이었네.’

죽을 뻔한 자신을 구해 준 사부를 철저히 이용하고 버렸다. 이야기를 들어 보면 마지막까지 한 줌의 죄책감도 없었음이 분명했다.

나는 이 정도로 순수한 악의(惡意)에 가득 찬 놈이 있다는 사실에 놀랐고, 조필이 더 이상 이 세상에 존재하지 않는다는 사실에 안도했다.

“그런데 용케 살아서 도망쳤군요. 남궁세가 쪽에서도 예의주시하고 있었을 텐데.”

남궁세가, 무협 소설의 단골손님.

무려 구파일방과 비견된다는 천하오대세가에 속해 있는 남궁세가다. 모르긴 몰라도 도망자 한 명 잡아 죽이는 것쯤은 일도 아니었을 것이다.

누군가의 도움이 있지 않고서야.

“혹시?”

내 물음에 적천강이 담담하게 고개를 끄덕였다.

“창천검왕을 찾아가 부탁했지. 그것이 내 마지막 도리였다.”

제자는 사부를 버리고 떠났지만 사부는 그런 제자를 끝까지 지켰다.

정말이지 들을수록 기가 찬 사제지간이 아닐 수 없다.

“……대단하시네요.”

“대단? 녀석 같은 살성을 제자로 키운 것으로도 모자라 사사로운 정에 사로잡혀 세상에 풀어놓은 내가? 그건 어리석은 선택이었다.”

적천강이 자조 섞인 웃음과 함께 말을 이었다.

“창천검왕도 내게 그러더군. 후회할 거라고. 그 말이 맞았다. 지난 십 년의 세월, 매 순간순간이 후회였다.”

“만약 그날로 돌아간다면 어떻게 하시겠습니까?”

대답에는 망설임이 없었다.

“살릴 것이다. 그리고 다시 후회하겠지. 백 번의 기회가 있다 하더라도 그때의 나는 그랬을 것이다.”

‘그때의 나’는 그랬을 거라고?

의미심장하게 들리는 한마디였다. 지금의 적천강은 다르다는 뜻이기도 하니까.

‘혹시?’

어쩌면 십 년이라는 세월은 그 나름대로 준비를 위한 시간이었을지도 모른다는 생각이 들었다.

지금도 세상 어디에선가 악행을 저지를 제자를 직접 죽이기 위한 마음의 준비 말이다.

‘만약 그렇다면…….’

문득 뇌리를 스치는 생각에 나는 조심스럽게, 아주 조심스럽게 물었다.

“저기.”

“말해 보거라.”

적천강의 가라앉은 목소리. 모든 것을 꿰뚫어 보는 듯한 심유한 눈빛에 심장이 요동친다.

나는 마른침을 삼킨 뒤 입을 뗐다.

“제게 묻고 싶으신 것이 있는 걸로 압니다.”

애초에 이렇게 마주 보고 있는 것은 옛 기억을 회상하기 위해서가 아니다.

그는 나에게, 나는 그에게.

우리는 서로에게 묻고 답할 것이 있었다. 그리고 칼자루를 쥐고 있는 것은 내가 아니다.

“대답해 드리겠습니다. 뭐든지.”

“…….”

칼자루를 쥔 자, 적천강은 말없이 텅 빈 술잔을 매만졌다.

그건 끝이 정해지지 않은 침묵이었다. 일각? 한 식경? 아니면 반 시진? 시간이 얼마나 흘렀는지 알 수 없었다.

밖에는 찬 바람이 쌩쌩 부는데, 긴장감 때문인지 전신이 땀으로 흠뻑 젖었다.

그리고 마침내 긴 침묵이 깨졌다.

“……죽었느냐?”

잔뜩 쉰 목소리. 담담한 척 애써 보지만 여러 감정이 뒤섞인 물음이다.

내가 고개를 끄덕이자 노인의 회색 눈동자가 파르르 떨렸다.

“그랬군. 결국, 그렇게 됐어.”

무심코 술잔을 기울이려던 적천강이 이내 술잔이 비어 있다는 사실을 알아채고 허탈하게 웃었다.

“어느 정도는 짐작하고 있었다. 네 녀석에게서 본문의 흔적을 느꼈으니까.”

열화신단으로 얻은 공력 때문이다. 내가 적천강의 공력을 통해 그가 화왕임을 짐작했듯이 그도 마찬가지였다.

“편안하게 갔느냐?”

“그건.”

칠공에서 피를 흘리며 발악하던 조필의 모습이 떠올랐다.

선천지기까지 끌어 올린 놈은 나와의 사투 끝에 상반신의 절반이 날아가 죽었다.

내가 대답을 주저하자 적천강이 주름진 손을 내저었다.

“되었다. 괜한 것을 물은 내 잘못이다. 무인들의 싸움에 편안한 죽음이 어디 있을까.”

“고통은 짧았을 겁니다.”

“한평생 수많은 이들에게 고통만 주던 녀석이니, 그 정도면 분수에 넘치는 죽음이지.”

말과는 달리 씁쓸한 얼굴이었다.

만약 적천강이 조필을 만났더라면 그는 자신이 할 수 있는 최선의 한 수를 펼쳤을 것이다.

가장 빠르고, 고통 없는 죽음을 내렸을 테다.

‘어쩌면 그걸 위해 다시 세상에 나왔을지도 모르지.’

하지만 적천강의 목적은 이뤄지지 못했다. 조필은 옛 스승보다 한발 빨리 나를 만났고, 목숨을 잃었다.

과연 적천강이 어떻게 반응할…….

“빚을 졌구나.”

“예?”

“못 들었느냐? 네게 빚을 졌다고 했다.”

“아뇨, 듣긴 했는데.”

얼떨떨해서 그러지.

이렇게 쉽게, 간단하게 저런 말이 나올 줄은 정말 꿈에도 몰랐다.

이게 무슨 일인가 싶어 눈을 깜빡이는 내게 적천강이 말했다.

“누군가는 그 아이를 멈춰야 했다. 십 년 전 내가 했어야 할 일을 네가 대신한 것이다. 그리고…….”

돌연 적천강이 입술을 움찔거렸다. 마치 누군가에게 그런 말을 하는 것이 처음인 사람처럼.

잠깐 주춤하던 그가 마침내 입을 뗐다.

“미안하다. 일전의 섣부른 행동에 대해서 너희들 전부에게 진심으로 사과하마.”

나도 모르게 목소리가 튀어나왔다.

“헐.”

“헐?”

“아, 아닙니다. 너무 놀라서 저도 모르게 그만.”

“노부가 사과하는 것이 그렇게 놀랄 일이냐?”

충분히 그럴 만한 일인 것 같은데. 그리고 본인도 엄청 어색해했으면서, 뭘.

“……어, 그게.”

어물쩍 말꼬리를 흐리던 나는 일그러지는 적천강의 얼굴을 보고 얼른 말을 바꿨다.

“천하에 명성이 자자하신 화왕 적천강 대협께서 저같이 한참 어린 후배에게 직접 사과까지 하시다니! 적 대협의 호쾌한 성품과 겸손함에 저절로 허리가 굽혀질 뿐입니다.”

“…….”

“…….”

얼굴 표정 봐라. 지킬과 하이드의 싸움이 따로 없다.

나를 때릴지 말지, 극심한 내면 갈등을 얼굴 근육으로 표현하던 적천강이 이내 한숨을 내쉬었다.

“도무지 종잡을 수 없는 놈이군. 이만 물러가거라.”

“넵.”

“저 아이들도 모두 데려가고.”

청풍은 탁자에 이마를 박고 쿨쿨 자는 중이고 혁무진은 여전히 마당에 엎어져 있다.

적천강의 마음이 바뀌기 전에 잽싸게 짐덩이들을 수거한 뒤 2층으로 올라가려는데 잊고 있던 사실 하나가 떠올랐다.

‘아, 맞다. 화염신장의 비급이랑 검은 돌려줘야 하는데.’

열화신단은 이미 먹어 버렸으니 어쩔 수 없다지만 남은 물건들은 돌려줘야 한다.

“It is a little run-down.”

Fire King Jeok Cheongang.

“I see. So that’s how it ended.”

“Did he die peacefully?”

“That…”

I pictured Jopil thrashing as blood streamed from his seven apertures.

After drawing on even his innate qi, he had fought me to the death and died with half his upper body blown away.

When I hesitated, Jeok Cheongang waved a wrinkled hand.

“Enough. It was my fault for asking a pointless question. What peaceful death is there in a battle between martial artists?”

“His suffering would have been brief.”

“A man who spent his life inflicting pain on countless others received a better death than he deserved.”

He would have granted him the swiftest, most painless death possible.

How would Jeok Cheongang react—

“Pardon?”

Never in my wildest dreams had I expected those words to come from him so easily.

“Someone had to stop that child. You did in my stead what I should have done ten years ago. And…”

Jeok Cheongang’s lips suddenly twitched, as though he had never said anything like this to anyone before.

After a brief hesitation, he finally spoke.

“I’m sorry. I sincerely apologize to all of you for acting so rashly before.”

My voice burst out before I could stop it.

“Whoa.”

“Whoa?”

“Ah, it’s nothing. I was so surprised that it just slipped out.”

“Is it truly so astonishing for this old man to apologize?”

It seemed plenty astonishing to me. Besides, he’d looked incredibly uncomfortable saying it, so what was he complaining about?

“I cannot make heads or tails of you. You may leave now.”

“Yes, sir.”

“And take those children with you.”

Cheongpung was fast asleep with his forehead pressed against the table, while Hyuk Mujin was still sprawled facedown in the courtyard.

I desperately wanted to settle everything between Jeok Cheongang and me once and for all today.

The back of the giant known as the Fire King looked small and lonely.

“You deserved to die.”

Jangcheon had killed dozens in Anhui alone. There was no telling how many people had fallen victim to his Disciple over the past ten years.

“You called it Might Makes Right, didn’t you? You’re the same. In the end, you died at the hands of someone stronger than you.”

No one remained strong forever, just as no one remained weak forever.

Even Jeok Cheongang, a Supreme Peak master, was weaker than someone.

“What a pathetic fool.”

Jeok Cheongang drained his drink. His Disciple’s words from that day long ago seemed to echo in his ears.

*I have never changed. Not once, from the day I first met you until now.*

Over the past ten years, he had turned those words over in his mind countless times. That single sentence had lodged near his heart like a dagger and tormented him.

“Did you truly never change? Not even once?”

They had spent many years together. At times, Jeok Cheongang had been a strict teacher; at others, he had cared for his Disciple like a loving father.

No—he had believed that was what he had been.

But it had all been an illusion. If it had truly been otherwise, Jangcheon would have chosen a very different path.

Being born into this world was like receiving a blank sheet of rice paper.

A person passed through countless moments between birth and death.

When death finally arrived, those moments came together to complete a single painting. The painting Jangcheon had created was… entirely ink-black.

Jeok Cheongang had watched it from the closest distance, yet he hadn’t known.

“Cheon.”

The old man stared at the seat across from him, where a wineglass had been set. One by one, phantomlike figures appeared in the empty chair.

A child hunched over as he stuffed dumplings into his mouth. A boy clutching the wooden sword his Master had made for him, his cheeks flushed bright red.

His limbs lengthened, and his gaze sharpened. Before long, a tall young man stood glaring at the old man.

*Kill me.*

That day, Jeok Cheongang had been unable to answer his Disciple’s cutting words.

But if he ever met his Disciple again, there was something he had desperately wanted to say.

“I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.”

Whoooosh.

A cold wind slipped through the door of the old inn and brushed across the wineglass.

* * *

“Benefactor!”

I awoke to a terrible racket. Cheongpung, practically bursting with excitement, was bouncing up and down.

“This is my pavilion, so why… Ah.”

Right. This wasn’t the Jin Family of Taiyuan. It was an inn.

At the same time, the events of the previous day flashed through my mind like a panorama. It wouldn’t have been an exaggeration to say I had crossed the boundary between life and death.

Well, that aside—

“Stop jumping around. There’s enough dust in here already.”

“I’m allowed to jump today!”

How was anyone supposed to sleep through this?

Hyuk Mujin, who had been curled up like a shrimp in one corner of the floor, blearily opened his eyes.

“Is this… paradise?”

That bastard started talking nonsense the moment he woke up.

It was absurd, but then I remembered that yesterday, after trying to escape on his own, he had been knocked unconscious by a duck bone Jeok Cheongang flicked at him.

“You awake?”

“Captain?”

Hyuk Mujin’s eyes widened when he saw me. Then he sighed.

“So this isn’t paradise.”

“…What the hell is that supposed to mean, you bastard?”

“It was a joke. A joke. I’m just glad to see you alive again.”

“Says the guy who tried to run away on his own.”

“Come on. Why do you have to put it like that?”

Grinning shamelessly, Hyuk Mujin looked around. More precisely, he looked at Cheongpung, who was running laps around the room like a train.

“What’s all this commotion so early in the morning? What good thing happened to make him run around like that?”

“No idea. He says he’s allowed to jump today.”

“He must’ve eaten something tasty.”

“…”

It was obviously bullshit, but since we were talking about Cheongpung, its credibility skyrocketed.

Giving him a doubtful look, I asked Cheongpung,

“What day is it today?”

Cheongpung, who had been circling the room and driving me crazy, stopped dead.

“Benefactor, you don’t even know that?”

“…Let’s refrain from saying things like that. It hits ten times harder coming from you.”

“It’s the first day of the new year. New Year’s Day!”

Hyuk Mujin and I nodded at the same time.

“Ah, so it’s New Year’s Day.”

“Right. It’s already New Year’s Day.”

“I thought it was something els—”

“Yeah. A whole year has already pass—”

After a brief silence, a profound realization struck us.

*Ah. The Jin Family of Taiyuan.*

At that moment, Wipeng’s threat from before I left the family rang vividly in my ears.

That was a loaded choice of words. It also meant that the Jeok Cheongang of today was different.

*Could it be…?*

Perhaps those ten years had been his time to prepare.

To prepare himself to personally kill the Disciple who might still be committing atrocities somewhere in the world.

*If that was the case…*

A thought flashed through my mind, and I asked carefully—very carefully.

“Um…”

“Speak.”

Jeok Cheongang’s voice was low. His fathomless gaze seemed to see through everything, and my heart began to pound.

I swallowed, then opened my mouth.

“I believe there’s something you want to ask me.”

We hadn’t sat down face-to-face just to reminisce about the past.

He had questions for me, and I had questions for him.

We each had things to ask and answers to give. And I wasn’t the one holding the sword hilt.

“I’ll answer you. Whatever you ask.”

“…”

Jeok Cheongang, the one holding the sword hilt, silently ran his fingers over his empty wineglass.

The silence seemed as though it might never end. Fifteen minutes? Half an hour? Half a shichen[^1]? I had no idea how much time passed.

A cold wind howled outside, but whether from tension or something else, my entire body was drenched in sweat.

At last, the long silence broke.

“…Is he dead?”

His voice was terribly hoarse. He was trying to sound calm, but the question held a jumble of emotions.

When I nodded, the old man’s gray eyes trembled.

“I see. So that’s how it ended.”

Jeok Cheongang unconsciously tried to tip back his wineglass, then noticed that it was empty and gave a hollow laugh.

“I suspected as much. I sensed traces of our sect in you.”

It was because of the internal energy I had gained from the Blazing Flame Divine Pill. Just as his internal energy had led me to suspect that he was the Fire King, mine had told him the same thing.

“Did he die peacefully?”

“That…”

I pictured Jopil thrashing as blood streamed from his seven apertures.

After drawing on even his innate qi, he had fought me to the death and died with half his upper body blown away.

When I hesitated, Jeok Cheongang waved a wrinkled hand.

“Enough. It was my fault for asking a pointless question. What peaceful death is there in a battle between martial artists?”

“His suffering would have been brief.”

“A man who spent his life inflicting pain on countless others received a better death than he deserved.”

Despite his words, his expression was bitter.

If Jeok Cheongang had found Jopil, he would have used the finest move at his disposal.

He would have granted him the swiftest, most painless death possible.

*Maybe that was why he returned to the world.*

But Jeok Cheongang had failed to achieve his goal. Jopil had encountered me before his former Master could reach him, and lost his life.

How would Jeok Cheongang react—

“I owe you a debt.”

“Pardon?”

“Did you not hear me? I said I owe you.”

“No, I heard you. It’s just…”

I was dumbfounded.

Never in my wildest dreams had I expected those words to come from him so easily.

As I blinked at him, wondering what on earth was happening, Jeok Cheongang continued.

“Someone had to stop that child. You did in my stead what I should have done ten years ago. And…”

Jeok Cheongang’s lips suddenly twitched, as though he had never said anything like this to anyone before.

After a brief hesitation, he finally spoke.

“I’m sorry. I sincerely apologize to all of you for acting so rashly before.”

My voice burst out before I could stop it.

“Whoa.”

“Whoa?”

“Ah, it’s nothing. I was so surprised that it just slipped out.”

“Is it truly so astonishing for this old man to apologize?”

It seemed plenty astonishing to me. Besides, he’d looked incredibly uncomfortable saying it, so what was he complaining about?

“…Well, you see…”

I trailed off awkwardly, then saw Jeok Cheongang’s face beginning to contort and quickly changed my tune.

“The renowned Fire King, Great Hero Jeok Cheongang, personally apologizing to a junior as young as me! I can only bow before your magnanimity and humility.”

“…”

“…”

Just look at his face. Jekyll and Hyde were fighting it out right there.

Every muscle in Jeok Cheongang’s face conveyed his fierce inner struggle over whether or not to hit me. Eventually, he sighed.

“I cannot make heads or tails of you. You may leave now.”

“Yes, sir.”

“And take those children with you.”

Cheongpung was fast asleep with his forehead pressed against the table, while Hyuk Mujin was still sprawled facedown in the courtyard.

Before Jeok Cheongang could change his mind, I quickly gathered up the two deadweights and headed for the second floor. Then I remembered something.

*Oh, right. I have to return the Flame Divine Palm martial arts manual and the sword.*

I had already swallowed the Blazing Flame Divine Pill, so there was nothing I could do about that, but I still needed to return the other items.

I desperately wanted to settle everything between Jeok Cheongang and me once and for all today.

“Um, Sir Jeok. I’m sorry, but there’s one more thing I need to tell you…”

I turned back, my voice as tiny as an ant, then stopped short.

*Glug, glug.*

Left alone, Jeok Cheongang was pouring drinks.

One glass, then another. He placed the second wineglass before the empty seat across from him and began drinking in silence.

I watched him for a moment, then suddenly thought:

*He looks small.*

The back of the giant known as the Fire King looked small and lonely.

I quietly turned away and climbed the stairs.

* * *

Once the presence behind him had disappeared, Jeok Cheongang muttered,

“You deserved to die.”

Jangcheon had killed dozens in Anhui alone. There was no telling how many people had fallen victim to his Disciple over the past ten years.

“You called it Might Makes Right, didn’t you? You’re the same. In the end, you died at the hands of someone stronger than you.”

No one remained strong forever, just as no one remained weak forever.

Even Jeok Cheongang, a Supreme Peak master, was weaker than someone.

Yet some people forgot that fact. Drunk on their own strength—or on blood—they strayed down the wrong path.

“What a pathetic fool.”

Jeok Cheongang drained his drink. His Disciple’s words from that day long ago seemed to echo in his ears.

*I have never changed. Not once, from the day I first met you until now.*

Over the past ten years, he had turned those words over in his mind countless times. That single sentence had lodged near his heart like a dagger and tormented him.

“Did you truly never change? Not even once?”

They had spent many years together. At times, Jeok Cheongang had been a strict teacher; at others, he had cared for his Disciple like a loving father.

No—he had believed that was what he had been.

But it had all been an illusion. If it had truly been otherwise, Jangcheon would have chosen a very different path.

“How could rice paper be black from the beginning?”

Being born into this world was like receiving a blank sheet of rice paper.

A person passed through countless moments between birth and death.

When death finally arrived, those moments came together to complete a single painting. The painting Jangcheon had created was… entirely ink-black.

Jeok Cheongang had watched it from the closest distance, yet he hadn’t known.

“Cheon.”

The old man stared at the seat across from him, where a wineglass had been set. One by one, phantomlike figures appeared in the empty chair.

A child hunched over as he stuffed dumplings into his mouth. A boy clutching the wooden sword his Master had made for him, his cheeks flushed bright red.

His limbs lengthened, and his gaze sharpened. Before long, a tall young man stood glaring at the old man.

*Kill me.*

That day, Jeok Cheongang had been unable to answer his Disciple’s cutting words.

But if he ever met his Disciple again, there was something he had desperately wanted to say.

“I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.”

Whoooosh.

A cold wind slipped through the door of the old inn and brushed across the wineglass.

“Benefactor!”

I awoke to a terrible racket. Cheongpung, practically bursting with excitement, was bouncing up and down.

“This is my pavilion, so why… Ah.”

Right. This wasn’t the Jin Family of Taiyuan. It was an inn.

At the same time, the events of the previous day flashed through my mind like a panorama. It wouldn’t have been an exaggeration to say I had crossed the boundary between life and death.

Well, that aside—

“Stop jumping around. There’s enough dust in here already.”

“I’m allowed to jump today!”

How was anyone supposed to sleep through this?

Hyuk Mujin, who had been curled up like a shrimp in one corner of the floor, blearily opened his eyes.

“Is this… paradise?”

That bastard started talking nonsense the moment he woke up.

It was absurd, but then I remembered that yesterday, after trying to escape on his own, he had been knocked unconscious by a duck bone Jeok Cheongang flicked at him.

“You awake?”

“Captain?”

Hyuk Mujin’s eyes widened when he saw me. Then he sighed.

“So this isn’t paradise.”

“…What the hell is that supposed to mean, you bastard?”

“It was a joke. A joke. I’m just glad to see you alive again.”

“Says the guy who tried to run away on his own.”

“Come on. Why do you have to put it like that?”

Grinning shamelessly, Hyuk Mujin looked around. More precisely, he looked at Cheongpung, who was running laps around the room like a train.

“What’s all this commotion so early in the morning? What good thing happened to make him run around like that?”

“No idea. He says he’s allowed to jump today.”

“He must’ve eaten something tasty.”

“…”

It was obviously bullshit, but since we were talking about Cheongpung, its credibility skyrocketed.

Giving him a doubtful look, I asked Cheongpung,

“What day is it today?”

Cheongpung, who had been circling the room and driving me crazy, stopped dead.

“Benefactor, you don’t even know that?”

“…Let’s refrain from saying things like that. It hits ten times harder coming from you.”

“It’s the first day of the new year. New Year’s Day!”

Hyuk Mujin and I nodded at the same time.

“Ah, so it’s New Year’s Day.”

“Right. It’s already New Year’s Day.”

“I thought it was something els—”

“Yeah. A whole year has already pass—”

After a brief silence, a profound realization struck us.

*Ah. The Jin Family of Taiyuan.*

At that moment, Wipeng’s threat from before I left the family rang vividly in my ears.
